aldemar.headline: Warsh puts a September hike back on the table — and two new names join the book
aldemar.standfirst: Friday's Jackson Hole speech reset the whole rate path: the Fed chair said inflation "is running above our 2% target", that the Fed's "predominant focus right now should be on prices", and that he is impressed by the economy. September hike odds jumped from 35% to 57% inside the session, the 2-year rose 8bp and gold gave back 2.88%. Equities faded — S&P −0.25%, Nasdaq −0.52%, Russell −1.39% — but BAC rose 1.88% to 62.32, reclaiming the level it lost Thursday. Both books also opened two new positions this week: PLTR on Thursday around 184 and AAPL on Friday around 321. Both are carried here as PROVISIONAL — approximate entries, no stops or targets yet — so no R is shown until you confirm the fills.

positions.title: 3 signals on BAC, PLTR, AAPL — read before the open

items.html: BAC — BAC +1.88% to 62.32 as hike odds jump to 57% — the 62 break reversed in one session. Thursday's high-volume break looked like distribution; Friday bought all of it back on 20.9m shares, with a 62.56 high and a low of 61.36 that never revisited the breakdown. Gabriel recovers from −0.80R to −0.52R with the stop now 3.2% below rather than 1.3%; Aldemar from −0.66R to −0.41R, stop 4.5% below. But read the mechanism precisely, because it is not the one you entered on: this was rate-hike repricing at the front end, not the long-end steepener — the 2-year rose 8bp while the 30-year rose only 2bp, which is a bear flattener. Higher policy rates reprice a bank's floating assets fast and help near-term margin, so the trade works; a flattening curve eventually stops helping. The thesis is being carried by a different engine than the one in your notes, and that is worth knowing before the next add or trim decision. Note that with PLTR and AAPL now open, both books are carrying four and three positions respectively into a live Fed meeting — two of them without defined risk.

PLTR — PLTR entered Thursday into a +4.75% breakout — closed the week at 186.29. You bought the move, not the base: Thursday ran 178.98 to 185.93 on 24.2m shares, roughly a third above average, and Friday added 0.19% to 186.29 with a 188.37 high. An entry near 184 sits about 1.2% below Friday's close. The fundamental case is not new information — Q1 net dollar retention jumped to 150% from 139%, operating margin hit 38.1% against a 14.2% three-year average, and full-year guidance was raised to $8.154bn, up 82%, with US commercial revenue +149% to $764m under the "AI sovereignty" framing. Trefis makes the fair point that all of this was legible months before the stock moved, which means you are paying for recognition rather than discovery. That is a legitimate momentum trade, but it is the kind that needs its stop defined precisely — and this position does not have one yet.

AAPL — AAPL entered Friday near the session high, into the 9 September event and a CEO handover. Apple rose 1.63% to 319.70 on Friday with a 322.37 high — an entry around 321 is close to the top of that range and roughly 0.4% above the close. Three things are converging: the 9 September launch with a first foldable expected, iPhone sales up 21.7% for a second consecutive quarter above 20%, and John Ternus taking over as CEO on 1 September, with the stock already up more than 17% since his appointment was announced on 20 April. Services pricing was also raised — Apple TV to $14.99 and Apple One to $21.95 — which is margin support that does not depend on the hardware. The risk is symmetrical and dated: buying strength eleven days before a product event means the event either validates the entry or supplies the reason it fails.

positions.note: Signal changes the thesis, the levels or the size — earnings, a regulator with teeth, M&A, a ruling with a revenue line attached. Everything else is filed as noise on purpose; a real signal survives skepticism.

themes.title: The war goes quiet for the first time in three weeks

items.html: Crude essentially flat at 83.40 to close a week that took 4.05% out of it. No headline moved oil on Friday, which after three weeks of daily repricing is the story. The Iran–Oman interim corridor and mine-clearance framework remains the operative plan without a start date attached, and the market has settled into pricing it as a probable eventual outcome rather than a live event.

No new sanctions actions or shipping incidents reported since Wednesday's framework. The pressure campaign launched on the 24th has not produced a follow-up strike on a financial institution as Bessent previewed, and Tehran has not answered with the Hormuz shutdown Rezaei threatened. Both sides are letting the technical track breathe — which is the most constructive silence of the month.

themes.note: The transmission is oil → inflation → the regime call, and this week it broke in the friendly direction: crude −4% on the week and the war's headline risk visibly draining. But Friday made clear that this no longer sets the rate path. The Fed chair looked past energy entirely and pointed at prices and a strong economy, which is why September hike odds nearly doubled on a day oil did nothing. The war has moved from the first line of this brief to the background — and the thing that now decides your book is the September FOMC, not Muscat.

world.title: Jackson Hole flips the script: a hike is now more likely than not

items.html: September hike odds surge to 57% from 35%; 2-year +8bp, 10-year +4bp to 4.72%, 30-year +2bp to 5.21%. A bear flattener — the market repricing policy rather than term premium. Alan Blinder called the remarks forward guidance from "somebody who thought interest rates should go up." Two weeks ago the debate was whether the Fed had room to cut; it is now whether it hikes in seventeen days.

Gold −2.88% to ~4,530, ending a record run with its worst session in months. The debasement trade needed a Fed that was behind the curve; Friday delivered one that is leaning into it. This is the cleanest single-asset expression of the repricing, and it takes gold back below where it started the week.

S&P −0.25%, Nasdaq −0.52%, Russell −1.39%, VIX 14.43 — all three indexes still finished the week higher. Small caps took the hike news hardest, which is the textbook reaction and a reminder of where rate sensitivity actually concentrates. PayPal fell 12% after Stripe and Advent walked away from a $50bn acquisition; Marvell slipped on earnings.

weekly.headline: The war stopped setting the price and the Fed started — and the AI audit closed
weekly.standfirst: Three things resolved in five sessions. Washington launched its "economic D-Day" sanctions on Monday and crude fell, because the barrels were already blockaded. Iran and Oman then put an actual reopening mechanism on the table — a joint corridor plus mine clearance, permanent route inside 30 to 60 days — and oil finished the week down 4.05%. Nvidia answered the AI financing question with $96.2bn of revenue and a $108bn guide, ending the audit that had run all August. Then on Friday the Fed chair walked into Jackson Hole and doubled September hike odds to 57%. The book ends the week with one closed trade, both BAC positions recovered off Thursday's break, two new names added — PLTR on Thursday and AAPL on Friday, both still provisional — and a new question: rates, not war.
